title: Thiebou Yaap
localName: Thiebou yaap — thiep, riz à la viande
author: Aïssatou Mbaye
desc: The meat thieb her author calls badly underrated and much simpler than thiéboudieune — the one you make when you cannot be bothered but still want to eat well.
longDesc: A rice-and-meat dish built on a browned-onion base with no tomato colouring and no bouillon. Three onions, fifty millilitres of oil, a bay leaf, five cloves of garlic, half a bell pepper, a tablespoon of vinegar, two dried bird's eye chillies, a carrot, a turnip and pitted green olives. The meat browns first, then an onion and the other half-pepper are caramelised with it, about a litre and a half of water goes in, and it simmers an hour on low heat. The onion sauce is finished separately until there is almost no water left. Her colour comes entirely from browning the onions.
ingredients: 0.5 bell pepper — red, green or yellow
// No quantity is printed for the meat or the rice. See the note.
// Optional: 1/2 sugar, unit not printed in the source
equipment: Cocotte or second pan, for the onion sauce
steps: Heat the oil. Once hot, brown the meat pieces.
When well browned, add one sliced onion and the other half of the pepper, diced.
Keep caramelising, stirring occasionally. The onions must be well browned, even brown, to get a good rice colour.
Add about 1.5 litres of water and bring to the boil.
Salt, add a fresh chilli and a bay leaf, then leave it to simmer 1 hour on low heat.
Dice or slice the remaining onions. Put a little oil in a cocotte and add the onions once the oil is somewhat hot.
Meanwhile chop the garlic, pepper and chilli into a small farce.
Add the bay leaf and stir so it does not stick.
When the onions turn translucent, add the farce, salt and pepper.
Add a little water, then the vinegar.
Peel and dice the turnip and carrot, add them, mix well and leave to cook a few minutes on low heat.
Adjust the salt near the end. The sauce is ready when there is almost no water left.
Finish with the green olives, and serve with the rice cooked in the meat broth.
chefTips: Her colour rule is the whole dish: the onions must be well browned, even brown, to get a good rice colour. No tomato, no bouillon, no soy sauce — just properly caramelised onions.
The sauce is ready when there is almost no water left. That is the endpoint, not a time.
Brown the meat before anything else goes in the pot, and get it well browned rather than merely sealed.
Vinegar in the onion sauce is what keeps an hour of caramelising from turning cloying.
Her own framing: much simpler than thiéboudieune, and the thieb you make when you are feeling lazy but still want to eat properly. She is right.
Note her seasoning tip calls for half a sugar to lift the taste, but the source never prints the unit — half a sugar cube is implied and never stated.
Pitted olives at the end are not a garnish; they are part of the seasoning and they belong in the sauce.
commonMistakes: Under-browning the onions and then reaching for tomato paste to fake the colour.
Stopping the sauce while liquid remains.
Adding water before the meat has coloured.
Boiling rather than simmering the hour.
sources: Adapted from 'Thiebou Yaap', aistoucuisine.com, path /publications/thiebou-yaap. BYLINE: Aïssatou Mbaye. Date as printed: 26 septembre 2023; page metadata records a modified date of 2025-03-11, a DATE DISCREPANCY recorded as seen. Yield: NONE PRINTED. TWO-PASS on every listed figure. The page's own tags use 'thiep' and 'Thieb'.

Sauce ingredients as printed in French: '3 oignons'; '50 ml d'huile végétale'; '1 feuille de laurier'; '5 gousses d'ails'; '0.5 poivron (rouge, vert au jaune)'; '1 c. à soupe de vinaigre'; '2 piments oiseau secs'; 'sel · poivre' with no quantity; '1 carotte'; '1 navet'; 'olives vertes dénoyautées' with no quantity.

TWO PRINTED ODDITIES, reproduced and not corrected: '0.5 poivron' prints the decimal with a POINT while the prose prints 'environ 1,5 litre d'eau' with a French COMMA — both as printed, in the same recipe; and '(rouge, vert au jaune)' prints 'au' for 'ou'.

A SIGNIFICANT ABSENCE, confirmed across both passes: there is NO ingredient list for the meat or the rice. Neither is quantified anywhere on the page. The six servings above is editorial, and no meat or rice quantity has been invented.

DONENESS CUES as printed in French: 'faire dorer' and 'bien doré'; 'caraméliser'; 'Les oignons doivent être bien dorés voire brunes pour obtenir une belle couleur de riz'; 'lorsque les oignons deviennent translucides'; and 'Votre sauce est prête lorsqu'il n'y a presque plus d'eau.' The one explicit time is 'laisser mijoter 1h à feu doux'. NO TEMPERATURE is printed anywhere.

A SEASONING TIP WITH A MISSING UNIT, flagged: 'n'hésitez pas à rajouter 1/2 sucre pour relever un peu le goût' — the unit of '1/2 sucre' is NOT PRINTED. Half a sugar cube is implied but never stated, and no unit is supplied here.

CULTURAL REMARKS as printed: 'un classique de la cuisine sénégalaise trop sous côté' — sic, for 'sous-coté', badly underrated; 'Beaucoup plus simple à faire que le Thiéboudieune'; and 'c'est pour moi le thiep que tu fais quand tu as la flemme mais que tu veux te régaler quand même' — the thieb you make when you cannot be bothered but still want to eat well. She stresses getting the colour without 'ajout de maggi, de sauce soja ou autre artifice'. The page is categorised under 'Spécialité Africaine' and 'Ramadan'.

NOTE THAT THE SAME AUTHOR PUBLISHED A DIFFERENT THIEBOU YAP IN 2017, with a mustard-and-macédoine onion sauce and a microwave rice step. It is published separately at SEN008 because the two recipes genuinely differ rather than being revisions of one.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the meat and sauce gently.
healthBenefits: High in protein and iron from the meat.
No bouillon cubes, so markedly lower in sodium than most published Senegalese rice dishes.
Carrot and turnip add fibre and beta-carotene.
culturalNote: Every cuisine has the dish that gets overlooked because it is easy, and in Senegal it is thiebou yaap — the meat thieb that takes an hour instead of three and asks nothing of you but patience with a pan of onions. Getting its colour from browning rather than from a bouillon cube is a point of pride worth keeping.
